The aphorism is often misread as a sweeping law that all social life moves toward free individual bargaining, or as a claim that status vanishes. Maine meant something narrower: he restricted "status" to legal conditions arising from family relations (such as patria potestas), and described a historical tendency in progressive societies for those fixed family-based rights and duties to be displaced by individually agreed obligations. The team note is mistaken on this point, because Maine explicitly excluded conditions that individuals acquire or create themselves, so status was not a loose label for wealth, occupation or taste, and it was later writers who stretched the term to cover any social position.

CONFIDENCE: 85
